pr.title: gohcl/decode.go: fix decoding value slices
pr.description: Decoding a configuration document into a struct field that is a slice of non-pointer nested block values could panic with a slice index out of range error when the target slice's initial length was shorter than the number of matching blocks found in the document. The decoder now grows the destination slice as needed instead of assuming it is already large enough.

testCase.title: Decoding a config file with two repeated nested blocks into a pre-populated list field
testCase.preconditions: A target struct has a field representing a list of nested configuration block values (not pointers), and that field already holds one placeholder entry before decoding starts.
steps: Prepare a struct instance whose nested-block list field contains a single placeholder entry.
Author a configuration document containing two occurrences of the same nested block type, each with different attribute values.
Run the configuration decoder against the document, targeting the prepared struct.
Inspect the resulting list field on the struct after decoding completes.
testCase.expectedResult: Decoding finishes without error or panic, and the list field ends up containing exactly two entries whose attribute values match the two blocks in the document (the original placeholder entry is overwritten).

metadata.feature: HCL nested block decoding into struct slices

provenance.note: At base, decoding two blocks into a value-typed slice field that starts with fewer elements than blocks found indexes past the slice bounds; the PR's own added test case exercises exactly this scenario.

pr.title: Fallback to default timezone for mocked now
pr.description: When the library's 'current time' is mocked using a moment expressed in a specific timezone (without explicitly requesting that the mock also pin the timezone), reading the current time back without specifying a timezone should present it using the application's default timezone, not the timezone the mocked moment happened to carry.

testCase.title: Mocked 'current time' should honor the application's default timezone
testCase.preconditions: The application's default timezone is configured as UTC. A specific moment in time has been created and is currently represented in the America/Los_Angeles timezone.
steps: Set the application's default timezone to UTC.
Create a fixed reference moment in time, represented using the America/Los_Angeles timezone.
Instruct the date/time library to treat that reference moment as 'now', without explicitly pinning a timezone for the mock.
Ask the library for the current date/time without specifying any timezone parameter, and format the result as a timestamp with timezone abbreviation.
Separately, format the original reference moment converted to UTC, as a timestamp with timezone abbreviation.
testCase.expectedResult: The formatted 'current' date/time returned by the library matches the reference moment's UTC representation (the application's default timezone), rather than matching its original America/Los_Angeles representation.

metadata.feature: Test-time mocking of the current date/time

provenance.note: At base, querying the current time after mocking with an America/Los_Angeles moment returns the LA-timezone representation instead of falling back to the configured UTC default, as shown by the PR's added testTimezoneConsistency case.

pr.title: fix(hasProtocol): expand protocol relative url regexp
pr.description: A URL-classification utility that reports whether a string starts with an explicit protocol, or is instead a protocol-relative address (like '//example.com'), failed to recognize several valid protocol-relative forms: addresses with three or more leading slashes, addresses with whitespace between the leading slashes, and addresses mixing forward and backward slashes at the start.

testCase.title: Classifying protocol-relative addresses that have unusual leading slash patterns
testCase.preconditions: A URL classification utility is available that, given a string and an option to accept relative addresses, reports whether the string has a strict explicit protocol, an accepted explicit protocol, and whether it should be treated as protocol-relative.
steps: Call the utility on the string '///test.com' (three leading slashes, no scheme) with relative-address acceptance enabled.
Call the utility on a string that begins with a slash, then a tab character, then two more slashes and a host, e.g. '/<TAB>//test.com', with relative-address acceptance enabled.
Call the utility on a string that begins with a forward slash immediately followed by a backslash and then a host, e.g. '/\/test.com', with relative-address acceptance enabled.
For each call, record whether the string is classified as protocol-relative.
testCase.expectedResult: In all three cases, the utility reports no strict or accepted explicit protocol was found, but classifies the string as protocol-relative when relative addresses are accepted.

provenance.note: At base, the underlying pattern only matches exactly two leading slashes with no whitespace, so '///test.com', the tab-separated variant, and the mixed-slash variant are all misclassified as not protocol-relative; the PR adds exactly these cases to the test table.

pr.title: avoid compile-time dependency on modules named in derive
pr.description: When a schema module has redacted fields and derives an Inspect implementation, reading its @derive attribute at compile time was adding a compile-time dependency on every module named inside the @derive options, even when nothing about those modules is actually needed. This PR reorders internal checks so the attribute is only read when a redacted field actually requires deriving Inspect, reducing unnecessary compile-time coupling reported via mix xref trace.
pr.diff:
diff --git a/lib/ecto/schema.ex b/lib/ecto/schema.ex
index 7e52f245c5..f91a86c217 100644
--- a/lib/ecto/schema.ex
+++ b/lib/ecto/schema.ex
@@ -2390,10 +2390,12 @@ defmodule Ecto.Schema do
     on_writable_violation_default = Module.get_attribute(module, :on_writable_violation, :nothing)
 
     struct_fields = Module.get_attribute(module, :ecto_struct_fields) |> Enum.reverse()
-    derive = Module.get_attribute(module, :derive)
 
-    if redacted_fields != [] and not List.keymember?(derive, Inspect, 0) and
-         derive_inspect?(module) do
+    # Reading @derive makes every module named in its options a compile-time
+    # dependency of the schema. Keep the read last so it is skipped unless a
+    # redacted field actually requires deriving Inspect.
+    if redacted_fields != [] and derive_inspect?(module) and
+         not List.keymember?(Module.get_attribute(module, :derive), Inspect, 0) do
       Module.put_attribute(module, :derive, {Inspect, except: redacted_fields})
     end

testCase.title: Required field validation flags a changeset invalid when a mandatory field is left blank
testCase.preconditions: A schema-backed struct has a required text field. An update payload is prepared that omits this field entirely.
steps: Build a changeset by casting the update payload (which omits the required field) onto the existing struct.
Apply required-field validation for that field to the changeset.
Check whether the changeset is reported as valid or invalid.
Inspect the changeset's errors for the field in question.
testCase.expectedResult: The changeset is reported as invalid, and its errors include a 'can't be blank' style message for the omitted required field.

provenance.note: The PR only reorders how the @derive attribute on redacted schemas is read at compile time to avoid unnecessary compile-time module dependencies; Ecto.Changeset's validate_required behavior is untouched and long covered by its own test suite.

pr.title: Use `HashCode.getBytesInternal` in `combinedOrdered` and `combineUnordered`.
pr.description: The internal implementation of the hash-combining helper functions combineOrdered and combineUnordered switched from calling the public asBytes() accessor (which defensively copies the backing byte array) to an internal accessor that avoids the extra copy, as a performance micro-optimization with no change in the values these functions produce.

testCase.title: Computing the MD5 digest of a well-known short input
testCase.preconditions: A general-purpose hashing utility exposes a standard MD5 hash function that can hash a string using a given character encoding.
steps: Take the ASCII string "abc".
Compute its hash using the utility's MD5 hash function with UTF-8 encoding.
Convert the resulting hash value to a lowercase hexadecimal string.
testCase.expectedResult: The hexadecimal digest equals "900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72", the standard MD5 digest for the input "abc".

provenance.note: The PR only changes how combineOrdered/combineUnordered read bytes out of an existing HashCode internally; the standalone MD5 hash function and its long-standing test coverage in HashingTest are unaffected.

Instantiate the generated client against a known base address.
Invoke the generated method.
Capture the HTTP request that was actually issued by the generated client.

pr.title: refactor: drop redundant `continue` and remove needless_continue allow
pr.description: Several loop bodies in the HTTP/1 frame-dispatch code, the HTTP/2 client body-piping code, and the HTTP/2 upgraded-stream reader ended their final branch with an explicit `continue` statement that was already the last thing the loop would do anyway. These redundant statements are removed, along with the linter allowance that had been suppressing a warning about them, with no change in control flow.

testCase.title: Fetching a plain response body over a fresh HTTP/1.1 connection
testCase.preconditions: A minimal HTTP/1.1 test server is listening and will reply to any request with a fixed 200 OK response carrying a short, known body and a matching Content-Length header.
steps: Open a client connection to the test server.
Send a simple GET request for the root path with no request body.
Await the response headers and confirm the status code.
Read the full response body to completion.
testCase.expectedResult: The response status is 200 OK, the reported content length matches the body actually returned, and the fully-read body bytes exactly equal the fixed content the server was configured to send.

provenance.note: The PR removes control-flow statements that were already the final action in their loop iteration, so behavior is identical before and after; a basic request/response exchange (covered by existing integration tests such as incoming_content_length) is unaffected.
